claim: A recent study projects treatment failures caused by antibiotic resistance will lead to 300 million deaths and a healthcare burden of $100 trillion by 2050.
source: A recent study projects treatment failures caused by antibiotic resistance will lead to 300 million deaths and a healthcare burden of $100 trillion by 2050 (O'Neill, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to O'Neill, 2016.

claim: Antibiotic treatments of infections caused by antibiotic-susceptible bacteria never achieve a success rate of 100%, often failing to eradicate them unexpectedly.
source: For example, antibiotic treatments of infections caused by antibiotic-susceptible bacteria never achieve a success rate of 100%, often failing to eradicate them unexpectedly (Doern and Brecher, 2011; Weidner et al., 1999; Gopal et al., 1976; Ficnar et al., 1997; Forrest et al., 1993).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published studies.

claim: Laboratory studies have extensively characterized how large bacterial populations (e.g., ~10^8 cells in a culture) decline under antibiotic treatment.
source: Previously, laboratory studies have extensively characterized how large bacterial populations (e.g., ~108 cells in a culture) decline under antibiotic treatment; e.g., see (Nielsen et al., 2011; Ferro et al., 2015; Regoes et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous laboratory studies.

claim: The current deterministic model of pharmacodynamics states that the population dynamics of bacteria exposed to antibiotics follows a predetermined course and can be predicted deterministically a priori.
source: These studies have led to the current, deterministic model of the pharmacodynamics, that is, the population dynamics of bacteria exposed to antibiotics follows a predetermined course and can be predicted deterministically a priori; see (Regoes et al., 2004; Czock et al., 2009) and references therein.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies describing the deterministic model.

claim: Previous studies had experimental detection limits (e.g., >>100 cells) that prevented direct characterization of the dynamics of a small population undergoing extinction.
source: However, due to their experimental detection limits (e.g., >>100 cells [Nielsen et al., 2011; Ferro et al., 2015]), the dynamics of a small population undergoing extinction have not been directly characterized.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies with specific detection limits.

claim: Inoculum size as small as a few cells can produce infections.
source: Inoculum size as small as a few cells can produce infections (Jones et al., 2006; Haas and Rose, 1994; Jones et al., 2005; Tuttle et al., 1999; DuPont et al., 1989; Hara-Kudo and Takatori, 2011; Kaiser et al., 1992).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to studies on infectious dose.

claim: Survivors of antibiotic treatment are more likely to develop antibiotic resistance, making subsequent antibiotic treatment of the restored population more difficult.
source: Additionally, these survivors are more likely to develop antibiotic resistance, making subsequent antibiotic treatment of the restored population more difficult (Gullberg et al., 2011; Kohanski et al., 2010; Lopatkin et al., 2016; Dagan et al., 2001; Allen et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to studies on antibiotic resistance development.

claim: For bacteriostatic drugs, at increasing concentrations, the plating efficiency remained nearly constant and abruptly dropped to zero when the drug concentration reached the MIC.
source: For bacteriostatic drugs, at increasing concentrations, the plating efficiency remained nearly constant and abruptly dropped to zero when the drug concentration reached the MIC (Figure 1A); the grey line was obtained from a linear regression analysis of the whole data set below 0.75 × MIC (see Figure 1A caption for details).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and statistical analysis.

claim: For bacteriostatic drugs, almost every single cell spread on the plate grew and formed colonies at a wide range of sub-MIC drug concentration, and no cells formed colonies at (and above) MIC.
source: This trend indicates that almost every single cell spread on the plate grew and formed colonies at a wide range of sub-MIC drug concentration, and no cells formed colonies at (and above) MIC.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the plating efficiency data for bacteriostatic drugs.

claim: Colony size decreased at increasing drug concentrations for bacteriostatic drugs.
source: Additionally, we observed a decrease in colony size at increasing drug concentrations (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: For bactericidal drugs, at increasing concentrations, the plating efficiency decreased gradually from 1 to 0.
source: For bactericidal drugs, at increasing concentrations, the plating efficiency decreased gradually from 1 to 0 (Figure 1B); the grey line was obtained from a linear regression analysis of the whole data set (see Figure 1B caption for details).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and statistical analysis.

claim: The gradual decrease in plating efficiency for bactericidal drugs contrasts with findings for bacteriostatic drugs and cannot be explained by the deterministic model.
source: This trend contrasts with our finding for bacteriostatic drugs (compare the grey lines in Figure 1A and B) and cannot be explained by the deterministic model.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of experimental data and inference about model limitations.

claim: At ~0.6 × MIC of bactericidal drugs, the plating efficiency was ~0.5, meaning that approximately 50% of the cells plated formed colonies and 50% did not.
source: In the plate assay above, we found that at ~0.6 × MIC, the plating efficiency was ~0.5, meaning that approximately 50% of the cells plated formed colonies and 50% did not.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data from the plate assay.

claim: The plating efficiency of the second plating was about the same as that of the first plating, or in some cases, marginally lower, ruling out heritable resistance as an explanation for heterogeneous colony formation at sub-MIC drug concentrations.
source: Contrary to our expectation, the plating efficiency of the second plating was about the same as that of the first plating, or in some cases, marginally lower (possibly because cells were challenged with drugs twice consecutively). This observation rules out heritable resistance as an explanation for heterogeneous colony formation at sub-MIC drug concentrations.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data from sequential plating experiments shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: In the absence of antibiotics, bacterial colonies proliferated homogeneously, meaning that different colonies grew similarly.
source: We counted the number of growing cells in each colony and plotted the number versus time (Figure 2A). The colonies proliferated homogeneously, meaning that different colonies grew similarly.
evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse microscopy data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: With a sub-MIC level of a bacteriostatic drug, the number of growing cells in each micro-colony increased homogeneously and similarly.
source: The number of growing cells in each micro-colony increased homogeneously and similarly (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse microscopy data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The population dynamics of bacteria exposed to a bactericidal drug were highly heterogeneous, showing stochastic population fluctuations.
source: In contrast, the population dynamics of bacteria exposed to a bactericidal drug were highly heterogeneous. An example image sequence was shown in Video 3. The number of growing cells within micro-colonies at 0.8 × MIC of cefsulodin is plotted here; the result shows stochastic population fluctuations.
evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse microscopy data shown in Figure 2C and Video 3.

claim: Within a given population exposed to bactericidal drugs, some cells were killed stochastically, whereas other cells survived and divided.
source: Visual inspection of such image sequences indicated that within a given population, some cells were killed stochastically, whereas other cells survived and divided.
evidence: The claim is based on visual inspection of time-lapse microscopy data.

claim: Population fluctuations led to dramatically different dynamics for different colonies, even though they originated from genetically identical cells and were cultured under homogeneous antibiotic conditions.
source: Indeed, the number of growing cells in each colony fluctuated randomly over time (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 3A–C). These fluctuations led to dramatically different dynamics for different colonies, even though they originated from genetically identical cells and were cultured under homogeneous antibiotic conditions.
evidence: The claim is based on time-lapse microscopy data showing population fluctuations.

claim: Population fluctuations drove some colonies into extinction.
source: Importantly, the fluctuations drove some colonies into extinction (the light red-shaded area in Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse microscopy data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The extinction probability increased with increasing drug concentrations.
source: We counted the number of colonies that went extinct and plotted the probability of colony extinction at various drug concentrations; here, we are interested in colony extinction because it is equivalent to bacterial clearance, which means treatment success. Figure 2—figure supplement 4 showed that the extinction probability increased with increasing drug concentrations.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: At increasing drug concentrations, the death rate (ϕ) increased.
source: We found that at increasing drug concentrations, ϕ increased (Figure 2—figure supplement 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by single-cell analysis data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 6A.

claim: At increasing drug concentrations, the growth rate (λ) changed little, remaining nearly constant.
source: But λ changed little, remaining nearly constant (Figure 2—figure supplement 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by single-cell analysis data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 6B.

claim: Bactericidal drugs have significant effects on cell death, but not on cell growth.
source: Therefore, bactericidal drugs have significant effects on cell death, but not on cell growth.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the data showing increased death rate but constant growth rate.

claim: At low drug concentrations where the death rate is lower than the growth rate (ϕ < λ), the extinction probability P0 is given by their ratio, P0 = ϕ / λ.
source: We first considered the extinction probability P0 at low drug concentrations in which the death rate is lower than the growth rate (ϕ < λ). In this range, P0 is given by their ratio, P0 = ϕ / λ; see Equation A6.
evidence: The claim is based on the mathematical model (Markovian birth-death process) described in Appendix 1.

claim: The model prediction that extinction probability increases linearly with death rate, with the slope being 1 / λ, agrees with experimental data.
source: The solution P0 = ϕ / λ predicts that the extinction probability increases linearly with death rate, with the slope being 1 / λ (the solid line in Figure 2D). We sought to test this prediction quantitatively by comparing it with experimental data. Above, analyzing time-lapse microscope images, we obtained the probability of population extinction (Figure 2—figure supplement 4), and the death rate (Figure 2—figure supplement 6), at different concentrations of bactericidal drugs. Using these data, we obtained the relationship between the probability of population extinction and the death rate, and plotted it in Figure 2D. We found good agreement between the model prediction and experimental data (compare the solid line and symbols in Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of model predictions with experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: At the MIC, the growth rate and death rate are equal to each other (ϕ = λ).
source: Taken together, at the MIC, the plating efficiency is zero because extinction probability is one (P0 = 1), and the extinction probability is one because the growth rate and death rate are equal to each other (ϕ = λ). In short, ϕ = λ at the MIC.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the model and experimental observations about plating efficiency and extinction probability.

claim: At drug concentrations above the MIC, all populations eventually go extinct (P0 = 1).
source: Next, we considered drug concentrations above the MIC, where the death rate is higher than the growth rate (ϕ > λ). In this range, the model predicts that all populations eventually go extinct (P0 = 1 in Equation A6); this makes intuitive sense.
evidence: The claim is based on the mathematical model prediction.

claim: Due to population fluctuations, populations are expected to go extinct at various times at drug concentrations above the MIC.
source: Importantly, due to population fluctuations, populations are expected to go extinct at various times (Equation A5), meaning that the number of live populations (the populations that have not undergone extinction yet) decreases gradually over time.
evidence: The claim is based on the mathematical model prediction.

claim: At drug concentrations above the MIC, all populations went extinct at various times, as observed experimentally.
source: We tested these model predictions by repeating time-lapse microscope experiments at drug concentrations above the MIC. All the populations indeed went extinct at various times (Figure 3A and Figure 2—figure supplement 3D–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse microscopy data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 2—figure supplement 3D–F.

claim: The number of live colonies decreased gradually over time at drug concentrations above the MIC, consistent with an exponential decay.
source: When we counted the number of live colonies, this number decreased gradually over time (Figure 3B). In this semi-log plot, the decrease was linear (compare it with the dashed line), consistent with the model prediction of an exponential decay (Equation A7).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B and comparison with model predictions.

claim: The magnitude of population fluctuations decreases with increasing inoculum size.
source: It is expected that, with larger inoculum size, a population experiences less fluctuations (because demographic stochasticity gets averaged out). When we estimated the magnitudes of fluctuations by the coefficient of variation (CV), that is, the standard deviation divided by the mean, using our model, Equation A16 shows decreasing CV with increasing inoculum size, supporting the expectation above.
evidence: The claim is based on the mathematical model prediction (Equation A16).

claim: The magnitude of population fluctuations (CV) increases as the death rate approaches the growth rate.
source: Interestingly, Equation A16 also predicted that the magnitude of population fluctuations depends on rates of cell growth and death as well (Equation A16); CV increases as the death rate approaches the growth rate, meaning that population fluctuations become intensified when neither growth nor death is a dominant event.
evidence: The claim is based on the mathematical model prediction (Equation A16).

claim: Near the MIC, a population with relatively large inoculum size may still be prone to stochastic extinction.
source: This prediction, together with our finding above that the death rate approaches the growth rate as the drug concentration increases to the MIC (Figure 2D), suggests that near the MIC, a population with relatively large inoculum size may still be prone to stochastic extinction.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the model prediction and experimental findings.

claim: At low cefsulodin concentrations, all chambers became turbid (P0 = 0).
source: We found that, at low cefsulodin concentrations (to the left of the dashed line in Figure 3C), all chambers became turbid, meaning all populations grew. Thus, the probability of population extinction was zero (P0 = 0).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: At high cefsulodin concentrations, all chambers were clear (P0 = 1), indicating the MIC.
source: At high concentrations (to the right of the solid line), all chambers were clear (P0 = 1); thus, the solid line indicates the MIC.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: At intermediate cefsulodin concentrations, heterogeneous population growth was observed, with some chambers clear while others were turbid (0 < P0 < 1).
source: At intermediate concentrations (between the dashed and solid lines), we observed heterogeneous population growth; some chambers were clear while others were turbid (0 < P0 < 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Plating of the clear cultures on drug-free LB agar plates yielded no colonies, indicating population extinction.
source: Subsequent plating of the clear cultures on drug-free LB agar plates yielded no colonies, indicating population extinction.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental verification of population extinction.

claim: MIC values were higher at higher cell densities (inoculum effect).
source: MIC values were higher at higher cell densities. We note that the higher MIC at higher cell density (inoculum effect) has been observed previously and is being actively studied by others in the field (Artemova et al., 2015; Brook, 1989; Tan et al., 2012; Karslake et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D and citations to previous studies.

claim: Stochastic clearance occurs even for a population starting with as large as ~20,000 cells, inoculum size much larger than infectious doses for many infectious diseases.
source: Figure 3D shows that stochastic clearance occurs even for a population starting with as large as ~20,000 cells, inoculum size much larger than infectious doses for many infectious diseases.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The extinction probability is determined by the ratio of the death and growth rates (P0 = ϕ /λ).
source: Our model indicates that the extinction probability is determined by the ratio of the death and growth rates (P0 = ϕ /λ; Equation A6).
evidence: The claim is based on the mathematical model (Equation A6).

claim: A reduction in growth rate should lead to an increase in the extinction probability.
source: Thus, based on the model, a reduction in growth rate (denominator) should lead to an increase in the extinction probability.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the mathematical model.

claim: Growth rate can be reduced by using poor growth media, or alternatively using bacteriostatic drugs.
source: Growth rate can be reduced by using poor growth media, or alternatively using bacteriostatic drugs.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about factors affecting bacterial growth.

claim: For a sub-MIC concentration of a bactericidal drug, either a switch to poor growth media or addition of a sub-MIC level of a bacteriostatic drug would lead to an increase in the extinction probability.
source: This means, for a sub-MIC concentration of a bactericidal drug (for which the extinction probability is less than 1), either a switch to poor growth media or addition of a sub-MIC level of a bacteriostatic drug would lead to an increase in the extinction probability.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the model prediction about the effect of reducing growth rate.

claim: Growth reduction (using casamino acids or adding bacteriostatic drugs) led to an increase in the extinction probability for certain bactericidal drugs.
source: The plating inefficiency obtained with these treatments was plotted as solid columns in Figure 4A. The rise of solid columns above white columns indicates that growth reduction indeed led to an increase in the extinction probability, in agreement with our prediction.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: For bactericidal drugs that kill only growing cells (kanamycin and 6-APA), neither the switch to poor growth medium nor addition of bacteriostatic drugs resulted in an increase in the extinction probability.
source: As shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2, killing was completely abolished for kanamycin and 6-APA, indicating that ϕ→ 0 when λ→ 0. As expected, for these drugs, neither the switch to poor growth medium nor addition of bacteriostatic drugs resulted in an increase in the extinction probability (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2 and Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: For ofloxacin or ciprofloxacin (quinolone drugs), the growth reduction strategy did not lead to a significant change in the extinction probability.
source: Furthermore, our model does not consider specific drug-drug interactions. For example, a previous study showed bacteriostatic translation-inhibiting drugs and bactericidal quinolone drugs affect gene expression in a way to negate their effects (Bollenbach et al., 2009). Consistent with this study, we failed to observe significant changes in the extinction probability when ofloxacin or ciprofloxacin (quinolone drugs) is used with and without bacteriostatic translation-inhibiting drugs (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4 and citation to a previous study.

claim: Antibiotic-resistant bacteria exhibited non-zero plating inefficiency at sub-MIC concentrations of bactericidal drugs, indicating stochastic clearance.
source: These resistant strains exhibited non-zero plating inefficiency at sub-MIC concentrations of bactericidal drugs (white columns in Figure 4B), indicating stochastic clearance.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The growth reduction strategy facilitated the clearance of antibiotic-resistant bacteria at sub-MIC concentrations.
source: We then repeated the experiments either by replacing LB with casamino acids or by adding a sub-MIC concentration of a bacteriostatic drug. As with the antibiotic-susceptible strain, these treatments led to an increase in the plating inefficiency (Figure 4B), indicating that our growth reduction strategy facilitated the clearance of antibiotic-resistant bacteria at sub-MIC concentrations.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Antibiotics known to kill bacteria (bactericidal) induced population fluctuations.
source: Antibiotics known to kill bacteria (bactericidal) induced population fluctuations.
evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse microscopy data showing population fluctuations (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 3).

claim: At high antibiotic concentrations, the dynamics of bacterial clearance were heterogeneous.
source: Thus, at high antibiotic concentrations, the dynamics of bacterial clearance were heterogeneous.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing variable extinction times (Figure 3A, Figure 3B).

claim: At low antibiotic concentrations, clearance still occurred with a non-zero probability.
source: At low concentrations, clearance still occurred with a non-zero probability.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing stochastic extinction at sub-MIC concentrations (Figure 2C, Figure 3C, Figure 3D).

claim: The striking outcomes of population fluctuations were well captured by the probabilistic model.
source: These striking outcomes of population fluctuations were well captured by our probabilistic model.
evidence: The claim is supported by the agreement between model predictions and experimental data (Figure 2D, Figure 3B).

claim: The model suggested a strategy to facilitate eradication by increasing extinction probability.
source: Our model further suggested a strategy to facilitate eradication by increasing extinction probability.
evidence: The claim is based on the model prediction that reducing growth rate increases extinction probability.

claim: The prediction for increasing extinction probability was experimentally tested for antibiotic-susceptible and clinically-isolated resistant bacteria.
source: We experimentally tested this prediction for antibiotic-susceptible and clinically-isolated resistant bacteria.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4B.

claim: The new knowledge exposes fundamental limits in our ability to predict bacterial eradication.
source: This new knowledge exposes fundamental limits in our ability to predict bacterial eradication.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the stochastic nature of bacterial clearance demonstrated in the study.

claim: The study demonstrates the potential of using antibiotic concentrations that were previously deemed inefficacious to eradicate bacteria.
source: Additionally, it demonstrates the potential of using antibiotic concentrations that were previously deemed inefficacious to eradicate bacteria.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing stochastic clearance at sub-MIC concentrations and increased clearance with growth reduction strategies.

claim: Experiments were conducted using E. coli strain NCM3722.
source: Experiments were conducted using E. coli strain NCM3722 (Soupene et al., 2003; Lyons et al., 2011; Brown and Jun, 2015).
evidence: The claim is a statement of experimental methods with citations to strain references.

claim: Bacteria were grown in 5 mL of Lysogeny Broth (LB, Fisher Bioreagents) in 20 mL borosilicate glass culture tubes at 37° C with shaking (250 rpm).
source: Bacteria were grown in 5 mL of Lysogeny Broth (LB, Fisher Bioreagents) in 20 mL borosilicate glass culture tubes at 37° C with shaking (250 rpm).
evidence: The claim is a statement of experimental methods.

claim: A rifampicin-resistant mutant (EMK32) was evolved from the WT strain with an MIC of 160 μg/ml.
source: We evolved a rifampicin-resistant mutant from our WT strain (NCM3722). We plated ~108 WT cells on a LB agar plate containing 20 μg/ml (2 × MICWT). 18 colonies were formed next day. We chose one colony and purified it by re-streaking. The mutant (EMK32) had the MIC of 160 μg/ml.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental evolution and characterization of a resistant mutant.

claim: Cefsulodin-resistant strain (EMK35) had an MIC of 170 μg/ml.
source: We obtained the cefsulodin-resistant strain (EMK35, MIC = 170 μg/ml) and vancomycin-resistant strain (EMK36, MIC = 250 μg/ml) from Georgia Emerging Infections Program MuGSI collection (their MuGSI strain numbers were Mu519 and Mu107, respectively.)
evidence: The claim is a statement of experimental materials and their characteristics.

claim: Vancomycin-resistant strain (EMK36) had an MIC of 250 μg/ml.
source: We obtained the cefsulodin-resistant strain (EMK35, MIC = 170 μg/ml) and vancomycin-resistant strain (EMK36, MIC = 250 μg/ml) from Georgia Emerging Infections Program MuGSI collection (their MuGSI strain numbers were Mu519 and Mu107, respectively.)
evidence: The claim is a statement of experimental materials and their characteristics.

claim: The deterministic framework successfully captures the reproducible dynamics of a large bacterial population declining to a small population under antibiotic treatments.
source: This deterministic framework successfully captures the reproducible dynamics of a large bacterial population declining to a small population under antibiotic treatments.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge from previous studies.

claim: The deterministic knowledge obtained from previous studies of large bacterial populations cannot be extrapolated to population extinction.
source: Our work demonstrates that the deterministic knowledge obtained from previous studies of large bacterial populations cannot be extrapolated to population extinction.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental findings showing stochastic extinction dynamics.

claim: The Markovian birth-death model quantitatively accounted for the probabilistic occurrence of population extinction.
source: We found that the Markovian birth-death model quantitatively accounted for the probabilistic occurrence of population extinction.
evidence: The claim is supported by the agreement between model predictions and experimental data (Figure 2D, Figure 3B).

claim: It is possible to increase the probability of clearance by manipulating population fluctuations.
source: However, this disadvantage can be minimized by manipulating population fluctuations and thereby increasing the probability of extinction. In the present study, we explored this possibility with the help of the probabilistic model, showing that it is possible to increase the probability of clearance.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing increased extinction probability with growth reduction strategies (Figure 4A, Figure 4B).

claim: Cell-to-cell variability in gene expression could be one possible molecular-level mechanism that gives rise to population fluctuations.
source: One possible molecular-level mechanism that gives rise to population fluctuations could be cell-to-cell variability in gene expression. Previous studies showed that variation in expression of antibiotic-resistance genes, marA, cat, kagG, ompC or bla, results in variation in antibiotic susceptibility to carbenicillin, chloramphenicol, isoniazid, kanamycin or ceftriaxone, respectively (Deris et al., 2013; El Meouche et al., 2016; Wakamoto et al., 2013; SanchezSánchez-Romero and Casadesus, 2014; Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on citations to previous studies showing gene expression variability.

claim: At sub-MIC drug concentrations, bacterial populations may or may not go extinct.
source: At sub-MIC drug concentrations, bacterial populations may or may not go extinct.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing stochastic extinction at sub-MIC concentrations.

claim: At drug concentrations above the MIC, all populations eventually go extinct, but not all at once, with highly variable extinction times.
source: At drug concentrations above the MIC, all populations eventually go extinct, but not all at once. Rather, the extinction time is highly variable, meaning that in some cases, it can take significantly longer to eradicate bacteria.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing variable extinction times (Figure 3A, Figure 3B).

claim: Inherent stochasticity, together with host variability, makes it difficult (or even impossible) to deterministically predict antibiotic-mediated clearance of bacterial infection.
source: This inherent stochasticity, together with host variability, makes it difficult (or even impossible) to deterministically predict antibiotic-mediated clearance of bacterial infection.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental findings on stochastic extinction dynamics.

claim: If tens of cells (or even a few cells) happen to stochastically survive a fixed course of antibiotic treatment, this small population can re-establish infections once antibiotics are removed, leading to treatment failure.
source: This means that if tens of cells (or even a few cells) happen to stochastically survive a fixed course of antibiotic treatment, this small population can re-establish infections once antibiotics are removed, leading to treatment failure.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental findings and knowledge about infectious doses.

claim: The observation of stochastic extinction dynamics has significant bearing on the issue of antibiotic treatment duration.
source: Importantly, a recent article raised an issue regarding the conventional wisdom of 'complete the prescribed course', and argued for re-consideration of antibiotic duration (Llewelyn et al., 2017). We believe that our observation of stochastic extinction dynamics, especially inherent variability in extinction time, has significant bearing on this issue.
evidence: The claim is speculative, connecting the study's findings to a broader clinical issue discussed in a cited article.

claim: Antibiotic-resistant bacteria have very high MICs, often above the levels that are toxic to hosts.
source: Antibiotic-resistant bacteria have very high MICs, often above the levels that are toxic to hosts.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about antibiotic resistance.

claim: Like antibiotic-susceptible bacteria, resistant bacteria exhibited non-zero plating inefficiency below the MIC, indicating a non-zero probability of clearance at sub-MIC drug concentrations.
source: Our plate assay using bactericidal drugs revealed that, like antibiotic-susceptible bacteria, resistant bacteria exhibited non-zero plating inefficiency below the MIC, indicating a non-zero probability of clearance at sub-MIC drug concentrations.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The probability of clearance for antibiotic-resistant bacteria could be manipulated, facilitating their clearance.
source: We also showed that this probability of clearance could be manipulated, facilitating the clearance of antibiotic-resistant bacteria.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: MIC is the most critical parameter to assess antibiotic efficacy.
source: MIC is the most critical parameter to assess antibiotic efficacy.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge in pharmacodynamics.

claim: In both deterministic and stochastic frameworks, at the MIC, the condition ϕ = λ is satisfied, but population dynamics are very different (population maintenance versus population extinction).
source: Therefore, in both deterministic and stochastic frameworks, at the MIC, the condition, ϕ = λ, is satisfied, but population dynamics are very different (population maintenance versus population extinction).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the comparison of deterministic and stochastic models.

claim: Dormant cells (persisters) are present in very low frequencies (typically 10^-5, meaning 1 out of 10^5 cells) and thus have little effects on population dynamics in small populations considered in this study (<<10^5).
source: Dormant cells are refractory to antibiotics, persisting through antibiotic treatments (Allison et al., 2011; Balaban et al., 2004). They are present in very low frequencies (typically 10−5, meaning 1 out of 105 cells) (Lewis, 2010), and thus have little effects on population dynamics in small populations considered here (<<105).
evidence: The claim is based on citations to previous studies on persister frequencies and inference about their relevance to the current study.

claim: The inherently stochastic nature of a small population may lead to variability in the process of enrichment and characterization of persisters.
source: The inherently stochastic nature of a small population may lead to variability in this process of enrichment and characterization, complicating studies of persisters. In fact, such variability was reported by a recent quantitative study of persistence (Brauner et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is speculative, connecting the study's findings to persister research, with support from a citation.

claim: The findings on the dynamics of small populations could be useful for a better understanding of persistence.
source: Therefore, our findings on the dynamics of small populations could be useful for a better understanding of persistence.
evidence: The claim is speculative about the potential application of the study's findings.

claim: In the deterministic framework, MIC is defined as the drug concentration at which the population size is maintained, which is realized when the death rate is equal to growth rate (ϕ = λ).
source: In the deterministic framework, MIC is defined as the drug concentration at which the population size is maintained, which is realized when the death rate is equal to growth rate (ϕ = λ); see Equation A2.
evidence: The claim is based on the deterministic model described in the manuscript.

claim: In the stochastic framework, at the MIC, the rates of death and growth are equal (ϕ = λ) and the extinction probability is 1.
source: Above, we found that in the stochastic framework, at the MIC, the rates of death and growth are equal (ϕ = λ; see Figure 2D) and the extinction probability is 1 (Equation A6), meaning all populations go extinct at the MIC.
evidence: The claim is based on the stochastic model and experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The clarification about MIC can reconcile two common ways to determine the MIC: a plate assay based on complete colony extinction and a broth method based on no change in culture turbidity.
source: This clarification can reconcile two common ways to determine the MIC, a plate assay based on complete colony extinction and a broth method based on no change in culture turbidity (population maintenance); although the MICs were determined based on different population dynamics in these two cases, both methods identify the drug concentration at which growth rate is equal to death as the MIC.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the comparison of deterministic and stochastic frameworks.

claim: With small culture volumes (which include a few or tens of bacterial cells), MIC should be defined based on population extinction, not population maintenance.
source: This clarification is particularly important in light of recent efforts to increase the efficiency of the broth method by using small culture volumes (which include a few or tens of bacterial cells) (Avesar et al., 2017). With such small volumes, MIC should be defined based on population extinction, not population maintenance.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the study's findings and cited work on small-volume methods.

claim: All live cells that stopped growing eventually underwent lysis in the experiments.
source: In our experiments, all cells that stopped growing eventually underwent lysis.
evidence: The claim is based on observations from time-lapse microscopy experiments.

claim: The variation in the number of cells in each chamber was ~10% or less when distributing cell culture equally to chambers.
source: Please note that although we prepared a large volume culture and distributed it equally to chambers, the number of cells in each chamber might vary. We found that the variation was ~10% or less. See Appendix 3 for details.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental measurements described in Appendix 3.

claim: OD600 of 0.4 contains 2 × 10^8 cells per 1 mL.
source: Previously, using a plate assay, we determined that OD600 of 0.4 contains 2 × 108 cells per 1 mL.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental calibration using a plate assay.

claim: The doubling time in LB was 18 mins and in casamino acids was 33 min.
source: The doubling time was 18 mins and 33 min respectively.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental measurements shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Kanamycin and 6-APA were not capable of killing non-growing cells.
source: We then stopped cell growth in cultures by depriving the cells of nutrients, added 1.5 × MICs, and measured SF. SF was one for kanamycin and 6-APA (blue columns), indicating that they were not capable of killing non-growing cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Other bactericidal drugs (besides kanamycin and 6-APA) were capable of killing non-growing cells, but with lower efficacy.
source: Other drugs (red columns) were capable of killing non-growing cells, but with lower efficacy as SF was not zero.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Lower susceptibility of non-growing bacteria to drugs has been previously documented.
source: Lower susceptibility of non-growing bacteria to drugs has been previously documented (e.g., see (Levin and Rozen, 2006)).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.
